hints: Notice the question asks which waves cannot be polarised, and recall that polarisation restricts the plane of transverse oscillations.
Connect the wave type to its oscillations: sound in air is longitudinal while radio, ultraviolet and X-rays are transverse electromagnetic waves.
Check that motion of the sound source changes wavelength by the Doppler effect but does not change the longitudinal nature of sound.
walkthrough: Identify the test: polarisation is possible only if a wave has transverse oscillations that can occur in different planes perpendicular to the direction of travel.
Recall the nature of each wave listed: radio waves, ultraviolet rays and X-rays are all part of the electromagnetic spectrum and are transverse.
Recall that sound waves from a moving source travelling in air are longitudinal, with particle oscillations parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
Argue that a longitudinal wave has only one line of oscillation along the travel direction, so there is no choice of transverse plane to filter.
Conclude that sound cannot be polarised while the three electromagnetic waves can, so the sound waves match the cannot condition. This is option B.

options.A: Radio waves are transverse electromagnetic waves, so their electric field oscillations can be restricted to one plane.
options.B: Sound waves in air are longitudinal with oscillations parallel to travel, so there is no transverse plane to restrict.
options.C: Ultraviolet rays are transverse electromagnetic waves and so can be polarised like visible light.
options.D: X-rays are transverse electromagnetic waves and so can be polarised.
